headline: Peconic Pushing Past 76 — Porgies Piled Up at Shelter Island, Bass Gone to Nightshift
subhead: The bay's run warm enough now that the stripers want the dark and the porgies don't care what time it is.
body_markdown:
By the end of July the Peconic has usually settled into its summer rhythm, and this year's no different — the bay warmed early back in May like it always does, and now in the last week of the month it's sitting well up into the mid-70s across most of the open water, pushing 78 in the shallow coves off Noyack and Three Mile Harbor by mid-afternoon. That's above the comfort window stripers like, and it shows in how they're behaving. We flagged this ten days back — said stable, warm weather would keep pushing the pattern deeper and more nocturnal, and that's exactly what's playing out across the whole bay complex right now.

Daytime bass fishing has gone quiet almost everywhere except right around dawn. The better action is happening after dark and in that gray hour before first light, with fish working the deep water off Plum Gut and the Orient Point rip on the tide changes. Guys drifting bunker chunks or live eels along the north side of the Gut on the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood have been finding slot fish in 25 to 40 feet, right where the current stacks up against the drop. During the day those same fish slide back into the deeper holes in Gardiners Bay — the flat off Cartwright Shoal, the hole east of Gardiners Island — and mostly sulk until the sun drops. If you want bass right now, fish the edges of the day, not the middle of it.

The good news is the porgy fishing hasn't slowed one bit, and honestly this is the time of year Shelter Island earns its reputation. Coecles Harbor, the flats off Cedar Island, and the drop-off outside Dering Harbor are absolutely stuffed with porgies right now, 12 to 15 inches with plenty of jumbos mixed in over 14. Small hooks, half a clam or a piece of squid, fished on the bottom in 15 to 25 feet on the last of the incoming through the top of the tide — that's been the money window all week. No need to overthink it. Chum helps but isn't required when they're schooled up this tight.

Fluke are stacked in the channels the way they always are once the water settles into summer pattern. The Sag Harbor channel, the deeper cuts off Jessups Neck, and the drop along the Greenport side of the bay have all been giving up keeper fish mixed with plenty of shorts. Four-inch white or pink Gulp on a half-ounce bucktail, dragged slow along the bottom on the outgoing tide, has been the most consistent producer — a couple boats working the channel edge off North Haven have put together limits of keepers to five pounds doing exactly that, working the drift right where the channel breaks up onto the flat. Bounce a strip of squid on the bucktail hook if the bite's finicky; it's made the difference more than once this week when the plain Gulp wasn't drawing strikes.

Weakfish are showing incidentally in those same deep holes where the bass are holed up during the day — nothing to plan a trip around, but if you're working bait on bottom in Gardiners Bay or the deeper stretches off Southold and you hook something that doesn't feel like a fluke, don't be shocked if it's a weakfish in the 16 to 20 inch range. Bluefish have been mixing into the bay too, chasing peanut bunker schools that have pushed in from the Sound side — nothing like the blitz action happening out on the ocean beaches this week, but enough activity around Orient and the mouth of the bay that a few boats working topwater plugs at first light have found choppers in the 3 to 5 pound class busting bait on the surface.

Tide-wise we're easing off the full moon push and heading toward neap, which usually softens the current enough that the fluke bite slows a touch on the slower stages but the porgy and bass fishing barely notices — those species care more about temperature and light than raw current speed this time of year. Wind's been light out of the southwest most days, which keeps the bay flat and comfortable but also lets that surface layer keep building heat, so don't expect the bass pattern to change much until we get a real blow to mix things up.

Looking ahead, I'd expect the status quo to hold through the first few days of August — porgies thick around Shelter Island, fluke steady in the channels, bass locked into their dawn-dusk-and-dark program. If a thunderstorm rolls through midweek like they tend to this time of year, it could stir the water enough to trigger a short daytime bass window right after it passes — worth having a rod rigged and ready if you see one building. Otherwise, fish the tide changes at Plum Gut for bass, work the Shelter Island flats for porgies, and drag bucktails through the channels for fluke. That's been the program, and there's no reason to think it breaks before the tide starts building back toward the August 12 new moon.
